notes:
I couldn't cover everything the brief asked for. I used up my searches before I found anything from Lutheran, Pentecostal/AG or Orthodox teachers, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter, so none of that appears below. The Guzik commentary on Enduring Word was also cut off partway through verse 10, so from verse 11 on I only have his comments that showed up in search excerpts. Where a site labels a commentator's tradition (for example StudyLight calling Gill a Calvinist Baptist), I've repeated that label.

**Overview (vv. 1–7)**
- Modern scholarship: the NET notes compare 4:1–7 to ancient Near Eastern *wasf* songs, in which a groom praises his bride's beauty from head to foot. The repeated "you are beautiful, my darling" in v. 1 and v. 7 frames the poem. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Sos&chapter=4
- Guzik (Enduring Word) reads the chapter as the couple's wedding night. The groom speaks almost the whole time, preparing his bride for their first intimacy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Methodist (Whedon) takes a different line, the "shepherd" reading. Here Solomon is a rival suitor, and the woman stays loyal to her country "Beloved" while she is at the palace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: he praises her with tender words that build her confidence, because earlier she doubted her beauty (1:5–6). He quotes Spurgeon, who hears Christ praising His church in return for her praise of Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Guzik notes that women in Israel did not normally wear veils except at engagements and weddings. The hair is compared to a flock of black goats flowing down a hillside, not to goat hair itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Guzik cites Trapp's allegorical reading, where the "eyes" are pastors and ministers. He offers it as an example of the danger of over-allegorizing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- NET notes: "eyes like doves" is probably about the eyes' shape and whiteness. Many Jewish and Christian interpreters have instead taken the dove as a symbol of a pure character. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Sos&chapter=4
- Whedon: the Hebrew verb is used of goats leaping playfully downhill, a picture of dancing ringlets. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the teeth are clean, matching and complete. He cites Poole's allegory, where the teeth are teachers who "chew" spiritual food for the people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- NET notes: sheep were washed before shearing, so the picture is white teeth. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Sos&chapter=4

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the lips are finely outlined and deep red. "Temples" includes the cheeks, flushed with colour, and the pomegranate means the fruit's outside, not its inside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- NET notes: the scarlet thread describes the colour and shape of her lips. The word translated "brow" can also mean cheek or temple. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Sos&chapter=4
- Matthew Henry, quoting Durham, reads the hidden "blushes" as the bride's modesty before God and her own conscience. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Sgs/Sgs_004.cfm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the point is not length. In the ancient world the neck stood for character, so this means noble, strong bearing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Reformed/Presbyterian (Barnes): the tower may be the one in Nehemiah 3:25–27 and Micah 4:8. The "tower of David" may be that mentioned in Nehemiah 3:25-27; Micah 4:8. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-4.html
- The allegorical readings differ on what the neck stands for. Matthew Henry makes it the grace of faith, which joins us to Christ as the neck joins body to head, with faith as our shield (Eph 6:16). This is generally applied to the grace of faith, by which we are united to Christ, as the body is united to the head by the neck https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-4.html
- Gill (Baptist) instead suggests the neck may be the church's ministers, standing just below Christ the Head. By the church's neck may be meant either the ministers of the word, set in the highest part of the body, the church, next to Christ the Head https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/4-4.htm
- Early readings (via Coffman): The Targum applied the tower to the Head of the Academy, and the weaponry they thought was the learning of the Law. (b) The shields were taken by Gregory of Nyssa to be the angelic guardians of the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-4.html
- Constable says the present "Tower of David" in Jerusalem did not exist then. What "tower of David" this was, we do not know. It was not David's "citadel," that now stands on the west side of old Jerusalem, because that tower did not exist then. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-4.html
- NET notes: the Hebrew word behind "rows of stones" (or "armoury") appears only here and its meaning is uncertain. Some scholars think shields hung on a tower showed warriors' allegiance to a king. Most link the image to shields lining the top of a fortress wall, compared here to layered necklaces, which fits the necklace mentioned in v. 9. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Sos&chapter=4

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the image is soft, gentle young deer. He also notes Clarke's and Poole's frankly physical readings, and Trapp's allegory in which the two breasts are the two Testaments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Whedon: red kids feeding among white lilies, a natural picture in Eastern poetry. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html

**v. 6 (readings differ sharply)**
- Guzik: the groom welcomes the wedding night. He grants that some see her breasts in the "mountain" and "hill," but prefers to read it as seclusion surrounded by rich scents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Bible.org (Utley) reads it plainly. This is a euphemism for intimacy. The mountain refers to the woman's perfumed breasts (cf. 1:13). https://bible.org/seriespage/song-songs-4
- Matthew Henry: This mountain of myrrh is supposed to signify Mount Moriah, on which the temple was built, where incense was daily burnt to the honour of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Sgs/Sgs_004.cfm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown read it as Christ's death and burial. Historically, the hill of frankincense is Calvary, where, "through the eternal Spirit He offered Himself"; the mountain of myrrh is His embalmment ( Jhn 19:39 ) till the resurrection "daybreak." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Sgs/Sgs_004.cfm
- Methodist (Whedon): the woman speaks this verse, not the man. He calls it the turning point of the Song: she rejects the palace and decides to go back to the countryside. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html

**v. 7**
- Guzik: the summary of seven praised features, seven being the number of perfection. He notes that the word for "spot" is often used of flawless sacrificial animals. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Gill (Baptist) explains "all fair" by justification. this is said to show her completeness in Christ, as to justification; and that, with respect to sanctification, she had a perfection of parts, though not of degrees https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/4-7.htm
- Matthew Poole warns against reading this as sinless perfection. There is no spot in thee; which is not to be understood simply and absolutely, as if the people of God were really perfect, and free from all sin Instead, God accepts them in Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/4-7.htm
- Coffman: The Jews, of course applied this to Israel. (b) Christian interpreters applied it to the Church, not the Church Militant struggling with sins and sorrows, but to the Church Triumphant in heaven https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-7.html
- Keil and Delitzsch: Certainly he means, no blemish either of soul or body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/4-7.htm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: he calls her away from her northern home and her fears, which the lions and leopards stand for. This is the first time he calls her "bride." Before asking for her body, he pledges her his life ("with me"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Methodist (Whedon): Lebanon and Hermon stand for the king's dazzling palace, which is dangerous for her. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html
- Matthew Henry: Christ calls His church away from the world. this is Christ's call to his church to come off from the world. https://biblehub.com/m/songs/4-12.htm

**v. 9**
- Guzik: one look from her changed him. "Sister" was an affectionate word for a wife. Spurgeon reads the two titles as "sister" by birth and "spouse" by choice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Methodist (Whedon): he takes the verb as "you have given me heart," meaning encouraged, and "spouse" as "my betrothed." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html

**v. 10**
- Guzik: she is not passive; she gives love back. This echoes her own words in 1:2. Spurgeon applies it to Christ valuing His people's love as they value His. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/

**v. 11**
- Whedon: her words are sweet as honey, the only sweetener people had then. Her garments smell like a pine forest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html

**v. 12 (the most debated verse)**
- Guzik: the three images praise her virginity, kept for her rightful husband. The spring is protected, not dried up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Ellicott: The closed or walled garden and the sealed fountain appear to have been established metaphors for the pure and chaste wife. He also cites a Jewish wedding prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/4-12.htm
- Methodist (Clarke) reads it literally: She is unsullied, a chaste, pure virgin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-12.html
- Gill (Baptist): the enclosed garden is the church, set apart by the grace of God, in election, redemption, effectual calling. His preferred sense is Christ's sole ownership of the church and her faithfulness to Him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-12.html
- Matthew Henry: the Old Testament church was enclosed and the Bible was "sealed" to one nation. but now the wall of separation is removed, the gospel preached to every nation https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-12.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown make the fountain Christ Himself. Jesus Christ ( Jhn 4:10 ) sealed, while He was in the sealed tomb: it poured forth its full tide on Pentecost https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Sgs/Sgs_004.cfm
- Coffman says these readings go too far. The item by item interpretations of Song of Solomon 4:9-15 are, for the most part, too fanciful to have any value. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-12.html
- Catholic: The application to Mary of a "garden enclosed, a fountain sealed up" mentioned in Canticles 4:12 is only a particular instance of a wider set of Old Testament figures for Mary. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15464b.htm
- Early church (Cyprian): he used the verse for the unity of the church. But if the spouse of Christ, which is the Church, is a garden enclosed; a thing that is closed up cannot lie open to strangers and profane persons. He argued that outsiders such as Novatian therefore could not baptize. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050675.htm

**vv. 13–14**
- Methodist (Whedon): "orchard" is literally "paradise," a word meaning an enclosure. The garden is "not merely enclosed, but worth enclosing," an imaginary garden stocked with exotic spices. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html
- Barnes (Presbyterian): The picture here is best regarded as a purely ideal one, having no corresponding reality but in the bride herself. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/song-of-solomon/4-12.html
- Matthew Henry: Saints in the church, and graces in the saints, are fitly compared to fruits and spices. They are planted, and do not grow of themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/4-12.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik: her purity is private, but its benefit is public, "a well of living waters." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: It springs upon earth; its source is heaven. It is now not "sealed," but open "streams" (Rev 22:17). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Sgs/Sgs_004.cfm

**v. 16**
- Guzik: This is the moment of yielded virginity, where the beloved is invited to enjoy the previously protected and sealed sexuality of the maiden. A line before, the maiden called it "my garden"; now it was his garden. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-4/
- Spurgeon (Baptist) reads the winds as the Holy Spirit. The bride acknowledges her entire dependence upon the free Spirit. The cold north wind brings out repentance; the south wind brings comfort. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons33/sermons33.iv.html
- In another sermon Spurgeon notes the change from "my garden" to "his garden." while we have but little grace, we cry, "my," but when we get great grace, we cry "his." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-16.html
- Matthew Henry: a prayer that there may be a plentiful effusion of the Spirit upon it, in order to its flourishing estate. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/4-16.html
- Speakers: Whedon has the man speak the first half and the woman the second. The Cambridge Bible prefers that the bride speaks the whole verse. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/song-of-solomon-4.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/4-16.htm
